label: Timothy Floyd Burchett
narrative: Burchett is the member who forced the modern UAP record into the open. He and Anna Paulina Luna drove the 26 July 2023 House Oversight National Security subcommittee hearing into existence; Ranking Member Robert Garcia thanked him from the dais for the leadership 'that has brought us to this place today,' and Jared Moskowitz did the same. Burchett opened that hearing by putting the first documented stonewall on the record: 'we were even denied access to a classified briefing in a SCIF prior to this hearing due to the amount of hoops that we had to jump through to grant temporary clearance to witness Grusch.' He then used his rounds to ask Grusch the questions no one else would - whether people had been harmed or murdered in the course of concealment (Grusch: 'Yes, personally,' and on murder, 'I have to be careful answering that question. I directed people with that knowledge to the appropriate authorities'), and what Special Access Programs cover the material and how they evaded oversight (Grusch: 'I do know the names'). Every one of those answers terminated at a SCIF the committee was not allowed into. He launched the bipartisan Congressional UAP Caucus in August 2023 and led a caucus letter to the Intelligence Community Inspector General; in January 2024 he brought roughly sixteen members to a closed ICIG briefing with Thomas Monheim and rated it a four out of ten - 'more of the same... it's very compartmentalized; it's like looking down the barrel of a .22 rifle.' He led the first push for a UAP select committee under Speaker McCarthy, which died with the speakership. He is the author of every standalone House UAP bill that matters: H.R. 8424 and H.R. 1187 (UAP Transparency Act) and H.R. 10111 and H.R. 5060 (UAP Whistleblower Protection Act). None have received a markup. His structural theory of the concealment is explicit and it is the theory this board is built on: 'You have to imagine Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the Manhattan Project, thousands of people working on the atomic bomb and less than 12 knew what it was.'
